records.sourceFile: Nutritional Interventions to Attenuate Quadriceps Muscle Deficits following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury and Reconstruction.pdf

paper.citation: Smith MJ, Hoffman NJ, San Jose AJ, Burke LM, Opar DA. Nutritional Interventions to Attenuate Quadriceps Muscle Deficits following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury and Reconstruction. Sports Medicine. 2025.
paper.abstract: This narrative review describes how quadriceps atrophy after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury and reconstruction may arise from disuse, altered mTOR and myostatin signalling, and inflammation. It then reviews nutritional supplements that might support hypertrophy alongside rehabilitation, and proposes a phase-based nutritional strategy. The authors state that the ACL-specific evidence is limited and that their strategy needs testing in ACL populations.
paper.tldr: Quadriceps atrophy after ACL reconstruction may respond to nutrition used alongside rehabilitation, but only seven ACL-specific supplement studies exist and they are mixed. The phase-based supplement plan in the review is preliminary.
paper.methods: Review based on Medline, Embase and CINAHL searches (earliest dates to 2023) with manual reference checks; the authors state that a systematic search strategy was not employed and no appraisal method is described. It is coded Systematic Review / Meta-analysis under the library rule for reviews that describe a database search. The review covers muscle atrophy and hypertrophy signalling, energy and carbohydrate availability, protein and amino acids, creatine, omega-3, collagen and caffeine, and summarises supplement studies in tables.
paper.findings: Myostatin was reported to be about 50% higher in ACL-injured patients than in uninjured patients, and disuse atrophy can reach 0.5% of muscle per day. Of the seven ACL-specific supplement studies cited, three (Laboute et al. 2013, Holm et al. 2006 and Shaw et al. 2019) reported some benefit with rehabilitation, and four reported no effect. The authors propose matching supplements to rehabilitation phases, such as whey protein after pre-operative exercise and 10 g collagen peptides during rehabilitative loading, but describe this as preliminary.
paper.limitations: The search was not systematic and study quality was not appraised, and the authors acknowledge that some relevant literature may be missing. The ACL evidence is small: one cited study had only two professional rugby players. The text reports Lopez-Vidriero et al. (2019) as showing no benefit, while Table 1 reports a higher IKDC score at 60 days in the supplement group, so the three-versus-four count of positive and null ACL trials depends on which is correct. The first author owns a company (Straight Up Performance) that produces supplements including collagen peptides, which the review suggests considering during rehabilitation.
paper.practicalImplications: Supplements should not be expected to replace rehabilitation for quadriceps atrophy after ACL reconstruction, because the ACL-specific trials are few and mixed. Meeting energy and protein needs is the review's base recommendation, since 5 days of low energy availability reduced muscle protein synthesis by about 30% in young trained volunteers (cited study). Any supplement trial with a patient should be agreed with the treating clinical team, given that the phase-based suggestions are preliminary.
paper.athleteDev: For athletes rehabbing from ACL reconstruction, the review's link between nutrition and quadriceps strength is mechanistic and preliminary. Energy and protein intake are presented as the foundation for recovering muscle, and the review does not test any sprint or performance outcome.
paper.rtp: The review addresses quadriceps recovery after ACL reconstruction and suggests nutrition as an adjunct to the clinical milestones that rehabilitation phases already use. It does not set return-to-play criteria, and it states that return-to-play nutrition is sport-specific and outside its scope, so it should not be used to judge readiness to return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Nutritional strategies in the rehabilitation of musculoskeletal injuries in athletes - A systematic integrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Giraldo-Vallejo JE, Cardona-Guzmán MÁ, Rodríguez-Alcivar EJ, Kočí J, Petro JL, Kreider RB, et al. Nutritional Strategies in the Rehabilitation of Musculoskeletal Injuries in Athletes: A Systematic Integrative Review. Nutrients. 2023;15:819.
paper.abstract: The authors update nutritional strategies for rehabilitation from musculoskeletal sports injuries in elite athletes, using a systematic integrative review of 18 studies. They conclude that energy balance, high protein and carbohydrate intake are the most supported strategies, and that evidence for supplements such as collagen, omega-3, creatine and vitamin D needs more clinical research.
paper.tldr: Rehabilitation nutrition for injured athletes should focus first on keeping energy availability adequate and protein intake high. Supplement evidence is limited to a few small trials, so supplement use after injury cannot yet be firmly recommended.
paper.methods: PERSiST-based systematic integrative review using the Whittemore and Knafl framework, searching PubMed/Medline, Scopus, PEDro and Google Scholar for English or Spanish studies published 2012 to 2022, with a protocol posted on Figshare. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 for trials and AMSTAR 2 for reviews. Eighteen of 3,736 records were included: five randomized trials, one cross-sectional study and 12 reviews.
paper.findings: Five randomized trials were included. Leucine (1.2 g/day, n=45 high-performance athletes after ACL reconstruction) was reported to favour recovery of the injured muscle, and creatine (n=18 adolescent fin swimmers with tendon overuse injury) was reported to support rehabilitation. Glucosamine (n=30 men after ACL reconstruction) did not improve outcomes, vitamin D (6000 IU/day for 12 weeks, n=21 wheelchair athletes with spinal cord injury) corrected status with an unclear effect on strength, and HMB (n=8, 4 per group, patellar tendinopathy) may improve power. Most included reviews advise avoiding energy availability below 30 kcal/kg fat-free mass per day and a high-protein diet of about 1.6 to 3 g/kg/day with 20 to 30 g of leucine-rich protein per meal.
paper.limitations: The evidence base is small and mostly narrative reviews with high risk of bias, and several included studies fall outside the stated inclusion criteria (adolescents, spinal cord injury rather than musculoskeletal injury, an injury-history survey rather than a rehabilitation intervention). The review excludes trauma such as concussion and focuses on treatment rather than prevention. Two authors hold supplement industry roles, including creatine-specific ties (science product manager for a supplement company that sells creatine, honoraria for creatine talks, and membership of the 'Creatine for Health' advisory board for Alzchem), and the article processing charge was partly funded by Galascreen Laboratories and DBSS International, both author affiliations; the review recommends creatine while declining to recommend HMB.
paper.practicalImplications: Monitor energy intake against energy availability during rehabilitation, since the authors advise avoiding values below 30 kcal/kg fat-free mass per day. Aim for high protein intake of roughly 1.6 to 3 g/kg/day spread across 4 to 6 meals, and check vitamin D status and correct deficiency. The review does not support a routine supplement protocol after injury: HMB cannot be confidently recommended, and collagen, omega-3 and creatine need injury-specific trials, so any creatine use should be weighed with the authors' disclosed industry ties in mind.
paper.athleteDev: Performance is mentioned only as background. The review notes that low energy availability can impair health and physical performance, but it does not test performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: The review is relevant to nutrition during rehabilitation from musculoskeletal injury, but it cannot set return-to-sport timing or doses for an individual athlete. The authors state that clinical trials in injured athletes are too few to confirm supplement doses.

records.sourceFile: One week of single leg immobilization lowers muscle connective protein synthesis rates in healthy, young adults.pdf

paper.citation: Holwerda AM, Weijzen MEG, Zorenc A, Senden J, Jetten GHJ, Houben LHP, et al. One Week of Single Leg Immobilization Lowers Muscle Connective Protein Synthesis Rates in Healthy, Young Adults. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2023 (published ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Within-person study of 7 days of one-leg knee immobilization followed by 14 days of ambulant recovery in 30 healthy young men. Deuterium-labeled muscle biopsies measured connective protein synthesis, and extracellular matrix gene expression, muscle collagen, plasma collagen markers and leg strength were also assessed.
paper.tldr: A week of single-leg immobilization lowered muscle connective protein synthesis in healthy young men, and synthesis rose during two weeks of normal activity. The study measured the tissue response but did not test any rehabilitation program.
paper.methods: Thirty healthy young men had one knee immobilized in a full leg cast for 7 days, with crutches allowed and no weight-bearing on that leg, followed by 14 days of free-living recovery. Deuterium oxide was given throughout, and biopsies from both legs measured connective protein fractional synthesis, mRNA expression and collagen content. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA compared legs and time periods.
paper.findings: During immobilization, connective protein synthesis was lower in the immobilized leg (1.07 ± 0.30 %/day) than in the non-immobilized leg (1.48 ± 0.44 %/day; P < 0.01). During recovery, synthesis in the previously immobilized leg rose to 1.48 ± 0.64 %/day (P < 0.01 versus immobilization) and did not differ from the other leg (1.32 ± 0.59 %/day). Leg extension 1RM fell from 56.7 to 49.5 kg and rose to 52.9 kg after recovery, still below baseline. Muscle collagen content and plasma PINP and CTX-I did not change, while collagen III, fibronectin and fibromodulin mRNA fell after immobilization and collagen I, collagen III, fibronectin, fibromodulin, tenascin-C and decorin mRNA rose after recovery.
paper.limitations: The immobilization lasted only 7 days, and the 14-day recovery is reported as an average, so the time course cannot be read from the study. Only healthy young men who were not resistance training were studied, and all received milk protein or peptide supplements from the parent trial (no group differences were found). Some samples were lost (collagen analyses in 25 men, synthesis in 28), and the parent study was supported by Nuritas Ltd.
paper.practicalImplications: The study supports the idea that a week of unloading lowers connective tissue remodeling in muscle, and that two weeks of normal activity brings synthesis back to the level of the other leg, while leg extension strength was still below baseline. It does not test any exercise, nutrition or loading protocol, so staff cannot set a rehabilitation dose from it. The authors speculate that resuming daily activity drives the early recovery, which was not tested here.
paper.athleteDev: The study gives a physiological reason to avoid unnecessary disuse, since leg extension strength fell from 56.7 to 49.5 kg in one week in these young men. It does not measure performance outcomes in athletes, so it cannot predict how much strength or training time is lost in a given sport.
paper.rtp: The participants were healthy young men with a cast on one leg, not injured athletes, and the study did not test rehabilitation or return-to-sport criteria. It cannot be used to set return-to-sport timing or loading, though it helps explain why short disuse affects muscle tissue.

records.sourceFile: Open fractures in National Football League athletes - Analyzing performance and return to sport.pdf

paper.citation: Nudelman B, Gardner BB, Bryant SA, Lansdown DA, Feeley BT, Pandya NK. Open Fractures in National Football League Athletes: Analyzing Performance and Return to Sport. Spartan Medical Research Journal. 2023;8(1).
paper.abstract: Retrospective study of 95 NFL athletes who had surgery for forearm, tibial shaft or ankle fractures between 2009 and 2018 (10 open, 85 closed), built from public injury reports and performance data. Open and closed fractures showed similar return-to-sport rates (90% vs 83.5%), career durations and performance changes, but the open group was small.
paper.tldr: In 95 NFL players who had surgery for forearm, tibial shaft or ankle fractures, open fractures (n=10) had return-to-sport rates and performance changes similar to closed fractures (n=85). The open group is too small to rule out a meaningful difference.
paper.methods: Injury, return-to-sport and career data were compiled from public team and media reports for NFL players with surgically treated forearm, tibial shaft or ankle fractures. Return to sport was defined as playing at least one regular-season game after injury, and performance was measured with Pro-Football-Reference approximate value (AV) against a two-season pre-injury baseline. Groups were compared with Fisher's exact, Mann-Whitney U and two-sample t-tests.
paper.findings: Return to sport was 90% (9 of 10) for open and 83.5% (71 of 85) for closed fractures (P>0.99). Median time missed was 48.9 weeks (range 35.1 to 117.4) for open and 43.0 weeks (range 2.4 to 108.0) for closed injuries, which was not statistically significant (P=0.17). Career duration (7.7 vs 8.0 years, P=0.78) and AV change in the first post-injury season (-0.6 vs +0.4, P=0.91) did not differ significantly, and the two-season post-injury AV change was -2.1 vs -0.5 (P=0.60).
paper.limitations: This retrospective design relies on public reports, and with only 10 open fractures the study had limited power, so a meaningful difference cannot be ruled out; fracture pattern and soft-tissue severity could not be classified. The Results attribute extra open-tibia time missed to a preseason re-fracture and an unrelated shoulder injury, while the Discussion names a serious infection and the shoulder injury; without these outliers the authors estimate a 46.0-week median (range 35.1 to 59.9). Text and tables conflict in places (closed first-season AV change described as a 0.4 decrease vs +0.4 in Table 4; 22 vs 20 closed forearm returners in Table 2; post-injury seasons 2.4 vs 2.0 in the Discussion vs 2.4 vs 2.9 in Table 3), so table values are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: For NFL players with surgically treated open forearm, tibial shaft or ankle fractures, counseling can state that return-to-sport rates were similar to closed fractures in this sample. Expectations should also note the small open group, the wide time-to-return range and that complications may increase return time.
paper.athleteDev: Average AV changes after open and closed surgical fractures did not differ significantly, which suggests similar performance outcomes for professional players in this sample. The result is a broad expectation only, since it rests on 10 open fractures and one public performance metric.
paper.rtp: Supports counseling that open and closed surgically treated forearm, tibial shaft and ankle fractures in NFL players had similar return rates in this cohort. It cannot predict an individual athlete's return date, since time missed ranged from 2.4 to 117.4 weeks, and the authors note results may differ in lower-level athletes or high-energy injuries.

records.sourceFile: Outcomes of Lisfranc injuries in the NFL.pdf

paper.citation: McHale KJ, Rozell JC, Milby AH, Carey JL, Sennett BJ. Outcomes of Lisfranc injuries in the National Football League. Am J Sports Med. 2016;44(7):1810-1817.
paper.abstract: This case-control study compared 28 NFL players with Lisfranc injuries (2000 to 2010) with same-position controls from 2005. Of the 28 players, 26 (92.9%) returned to NFL competition at a median of 11.1 months (IQR 10.3 to 12.5). Median change in power rating per season was -34.8 (IQR -64.4 to 1.4) vs -18.8 (IQR -52.9 to 31.5) in controls for offensive players (P = .33) and -13.5 (IQR -30.9 to 4.3) vs -5.0 (IQR -22.0 to 14.0) for defensive players (P = .21), so the declines did not differ significantly from controls.
paper.tldr: Most NFL players in this series (26 of 28) returned to NFL play after a Lisfranc injury, at a median of 11.1 months. Their power ratings fell after return, but not significantly more than controls in this small sample.
paper.methods: Injuries were identified from NFL game summaries, weekly team injury reports and player profiles for 2000 to 2010. Offensive players were compared with running backs, wide receivers and tight ends, and defensive players with linemen, linebackers and defensive backs who competed in 2005. Yearly power ratings (offense: yards and touchdowns; defense: tackles, sacks and interceptions) were compared for 3 seasons before and after the injury season using Mann-Whitney U tests with a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of P = .001.
paper.findings: 26 of 28 (92.9%) players returned to regular-season play at a median of 11.1 months (IQR 10.3 to 12.5) and missed a median of 8.5 regular-season games. Nonoperatively treated players (n = 6) returned at a median of 6.2 months vs 11.6 months for operative cases (n = 22, P = .02), which the authors call a trend and attribute more likely to injury severity than to surgery. The median change in power rating per season was -34.8 vs -18.8 for offensive players and controls (P = .33) and -13.5 vs -5.0 for defensive players and controls (P = .21); games played after the injury season did not differ from controls (offense 48 vs 53, P = .61; defense 50 vs 46, P = .78). Fourteen of 28 players exceeded their preinjury power rating in at least one postinjury season.
paper.limitations: Injuries were identified from public NFL reports without physical examination or imaging, so the diagnosis and injury severity were not confirmed. Severity, surgical technique and rehabilitation programmes were not assessed, and the sample was small (11 offensive and 17 defensive players; only 6 managed nonoperatively), so the authors note the study may have been underpowered to detect a mild decline. The extracted abstract text drops the minus signs on the change scores and IQRs (for example '234.8 (IQR, 264.4 to 1.4)'); the tables and discussion print them as -34.8 (-64.4 to 1.4), and those values are used here. Injured defensive players also had higher preinjury production than controls (median DPR 61.0 vs 44.0, P = .02).
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can tell athletes that most NFL players with a Lisfranc injury in this cohort returned to play, at a median of about 11 months, and that half exceeded their preinjury production in at least one later season. Expectations of a performance drop should be framed as uncertain, since the observed declines did not differ significantly from controls in this small sample. The shorter return after nonoperative care should not be read as an effect of treatment choice, since the authors suggest it likely reflects milder injuries.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use a season-level production rating as a simple outcome measure after a midfoot injury in football. The study did not find a significant change after return, so it should not be used to predict an individual player's performance decline.
paper.rtp: The study supports telling an NFL player that return to at least one regular-season game occurred at a median of 11.1 months in this cohort. It does not set clearance criteria or show whether specific rehabilitation or surgical approaches change return timing, and it should not be applied to non-football athletes or to midfoot sprains.

paper.citation: Gulgosteren E, Yuksel O, Gurol B, Yildirim O, Atar O, Soylu C, et al. Persistent neuromuscular deficits in the posterior kinetic chain following hamstring strain injury: EMG insights from Nordic hamstring curl, kettlebell swing, and supine sliding leg curl. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil. 2025.
paper.abstract: Cross-sectional study of 42 male football players (21 with a hamstring strain in the previous 6 months, 21 healthy controls) comparing surface EMG activation of the biceps femoris, gluteus maximus, latissimus dorsi and iliocostalis lumborum during three posterior chain exercises. The injured group had lower activation in all four muscles across the Nordic hamstring curl, kettlebell swing and supine sliding leg curl, with effect sizes from medium to large.
paper.tldr: Football players with a recent hamstring strain showed lower EMG activation in the hamstring, gluteal and trunk muscles than healthy controls during three strengthening exercises. The design cannot show whether this deficit causes or results from injury, so treat it as a finding to check, not a proven target.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional laboratory study comparing 21 male football players with a unilateral hamstring strain within the previous 6 months against 21 controls with no strain in the past 6 months and a straight-leg raise under 80 degrees; players with a professional sports background were excluded. Surface EMG (8-channel Noraxon, SENIAM placement, blinded analysis) was normalised to maximal voluntary isometric contraction (%MVIC) during three randomised exercises of three repetitions each: Nordic hamstring curl, kettlebell swing and supine sliding leg curl. Groups were compared with independent t-tests (Mann-Whitney U if normality failed), with no correction for multiple comparisons.
paper.findings: Injured players had lower activation than controls in all four muscles for all three exercises. Biceps femoris was 52.3 vs 76.8 %MVIC (Nordic hamstring curl, d = 2.08), 58.7 vs 82.4 (kettlebell swing, d = 2.06) and 48.6 vs 70.5 (supine sliding leg curl, d = 2.07), all p < 0.001; gluteus maximus gaps were largest in the kettlebell swing (68.9 vs 92.6, d = 1.87). Latissimus dorsi and iliocostalis lumborum differences were smaller (d 0.86 to 1.07, p 0.001 to 0.008).
paper.limitations: The cross-sectional design cannot establish causation. Inclusion only required a strain within the previous 6 months, and return-to-play status was not reported, so the abstract's claim of deficits 'even after return to play' was not measured. Injured players were tested on the injured limb and controls on the dominant limb, and no multiple-comparison correction was applied. The abstract's percentage reductions for the Nordic hamstring curl and supine sliding leg curl (for example, biceps femoris -23.9% and -20.8%) do not match the reported group means (about -32% and -31%), so the results values are used here; the abstract's claim that the largest deficits were in hip-dominant exercise holds for gluteus maximus but not biceps femoris (24.5 %MVIC gap in the Nordic hamstring curl vs 23.7 in the kettlebell swing).
paper.practicalImplications: Because injured players showed lower activation in both knee-dominant and hip-dominant exercises, staff could include both types when assessing or training athletes after a recent hamstring strain. The study does not show that restoring activation reduces reinjury or that a particular exercise sequence improves outcomes.
paper.athleteDev: Lower posterior chain activation after a recent hamstring strain suggests that the hamstring, gluteal and trunk muscles may not work fully in these exercises for some players. Performance staff can use these results as context for exercise choice, but the study did not measure strength, sprinting or change-of-direction outcomes.
paper.rtp: The study did not report return-to-play status or test readiness, so it cannot be used as a clearance criterion or as evidence that deficits persist after return to play. The authors suggest sEMG benchmarks could guide return-to-play decisions, but this was not tested.

records.sourceFile: Patellar tendon load progression during rehabilitation exercises - Implications for the treatment of patellar tendon injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Scattone Silva R, Song K, Hullfish TJ, Sprague A, Silbernagel KG, Baxter JR. Patellar tendon load progression during rehabilitation exercises: implications for the treatment of patellar tendon injuries. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2024;56(3):545-552.
paper.abstract: Twenty healthy adults performed 35 rehabilitation and sport-movement exercises while motion capture and force plate data were collected. A patellar tendon loading index, weighted 50% loading peak, 30% impulse and 20% loading rate, was used to rank the exercises, with the single-leg decline squat highest (0.747) and walking lowest (0.106).
paper.tldr: Patellar tendon load was highest in single-leg decline squats, run-and-cut and single-leg hops, and lowest in walking, low step-ups and 60-degree squats. The tiers offer an ordered loading progression, but they come from healthy adults and a model-estimated tendon force.
paper.methods: Twenty healthy adults (10 women, 10 men) with no lower-limb or spine injury in the previous 6 months performed 35 exercises. Twelve-camera motion capture (100 Hz) and three force plates (1000 Hz) fed a constrained sagittal-plane knee model, and patellar tendon force was estimated as knee moment divided by a knee-angle-dependent moment arm. Loading peak, impulse and rate were normalised and combined into a loading index, and exercises were grouped into three tiers (index of 0.33 or less, 0.33 to 0.66, and 0.66 or more).
paper.findings: The single-leg decline squat had the highest loading index (0.747; peak 5.2 body weights), followed by run-and-cut (0.725) and single-leg countermovement hop (0.711). Walking (0.106), low step-up (0.187), 60-degree double-leg squat (0.224), low step-down (0.288) and high step-up (0.321) were tier 1. The Spanish squat scored 0.563, mostly from loading impulse. Single-leg squats did not double the peak load of double-leg squats, and 60-degree squats produced about half the peak load of full squats (1.8 versus 3.4 body weights).
paper.limitations: Participants were young healthy adults, not patients with patellar tendinopathy or ACL reconstruction, and the authors caution against generalising to patients. Patellar tendon force was estimated from net knee moment with a sagittal-plane knee model, not measured, so frontal and transverse plane effects and hamstring coactivation were not modelled, and the Spanish squat relied on an assumed equal belt force. The weights and scaling of the three loading parameters rest on the authors' judgment, changing them changes the ranking, and the tiers have not been tested in intervention studies.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians can use the tiers to sequence loading, for example starting with lower-tier step-ups and 60-degree squats before full squats. The authors suggest the single-leg decline squat is not the best first exercise for tendinopathy, and that jumps and landings can enter at an intermediate stage, excluding the highest-tier hops. They also note the Spanish squat produces anterior tibial translation, which they consider contraindicated in the early phase after bone-patellar tendon-bone graft.
paper.athleteDev: The tiers can help order jump and landing loads within a conditioning progression. The study did not measure performance outcomes or use athletes.
paper.rtp: Limited to load ordering. The authors suggest ranking exercises by loading rate near return to sport, but the study did not test this or any return-to-sport criterion.

records.sourceFile: People Are More Variable Than Their Hop Test Would Suggest - Hop Performance and Self-Reported Outcomes Over 11 Years Following ACL Reconstruction.pdf

paper.citation: Girdwood MA, Crossley KM, Patterson BE, Rio EK, Whitehead TS, Morris HG, et al. People are more variable than their hop test would suggest: hop performance and self-reported outcomes over 11 years following ACL reconstruction. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2024;34:e14727.
paper.abstract: A cohort of 124 adults followed for 11 years after hamstring-autograft ACL reconstruction showed stable self-reported knee pain and quality of life on average, with wide individual variation. Better single-forward and side hop performance at one year was modestly related to better later KOOS pain, but hop performance was not related to subsequent knee events.
paper.tldr: Self-reported knee pain and quality of life after ACL reconstruction stayed broadly stable for 11 years, with large differences between individuals. One-year hop performance showed only small, group-level links to later knee pain and no link to later knee injury or surgery.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort of 124 adults aged 18 to 50 at ACL reconstruction with a hamstring autograft, assessed at 1 year, with follow-up at 3 years (n = 114), 5 years (n = 89) and 11 years (n = 72). Single-forward, triple-crossover and side hop tests were done at 1 year, but only single-forward and side hop were used as predictors because the two forward tests were highly correlated (r = 0.90); KOOS pain and quality of life were collected at each follow-up. Ordered beta mixed models estimated hop-outcome relationships, and Cox models related hop performance to subsequent knee events, adjusted for age, sex, BMI and concomitant injury with return to preinjury sport as a time-varying covariate.
paper.findings: Mean KOOS pain changed by 3 points or less and KOOS quality of life by up to 10 points (at 5 years) across follow-up, with large individual variation (ICC 0.67 for pain). Each additional cm of single-forward hop was associated with a 0.06% better KOOS pain score (95% CI 0.02 to 0.10), and each side hop repetition with 0.10% (0.02 to 0.19); for quality of life the single-forward hop relationship was present below 108 cm (0.36% per cm, 0.19 to 0.52) but not above it. There were 21 index-knee and 11 contralateral subsequent knee events, and hop performance was not related to their risk (index-knee HR 0.99, 0.98 to 1.02).
paper.limitations: Single-centre cohort with about 40% dropout by 11 years, and men were more likely than women to be lost (OR 3.55), so attrition bias is possible. Rehabilitation was not controlled, return-to-sport testing was not routine, knee events were recalled by participants, and sport type and competitive level were not reported. The text gives 11 contralateral events while Table 2 totals 12 (one participant injured both knees), and the abstract gives age as 31 ± 8 years while Table 1 gives 30.8 (8.7); table values are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: Hop testing remains useful for judging readiness to return to sport and for setting rehabilitation goals. For long-term prognosis, the authors suggest that the patient's current self-reported knee status at 1 year may be a better guide than hop performance. Hop results should not be used to tell an individual patient what their knee outcome will be.
paper.athleteDev: Not applicable to athlete development. The study concerns knee outcomes after ACL reconstruction, not performance improvement.
paper.rtp: Relevant to return-to-sport testing, but the study does not show that passing hop criteria reduces reinjury risk. Return to preinjury sport was not associated with later knee injury, and the authors say the impact of passing return-to-sport criteria could not be measured.

records.sourceFile: Performance and return to sport afte open fracture in National Football League players.pdf

paper.citation: Cotton MO, Sliepka JM III, Klavas DM, McCulloch PC, Harris JD, Jack RA II. Performance and Return to Sport After Open Fracture in National Football League Players. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2021;9(9):23259671211027862.
paper.abstract: Retrospective comparative series of 37 NFL players who sustained an open fracture between 1970 and 2018, each compared with one matched control. Thirty players (81%) returned to at least one NFL game after a mean of 9.3 ± 8.2 months. Career length, games per season and performance scores were similar to matched controls, and upper-extremity fractures were associated with faster return and better postinjury performance than lower-extremity fractures.
paper.tldr: Most NFL players with open fractures (81%) returned to play, at an average of about 9 months, with career length and performance similar to matched controls. Upper-extremity fractures returned faster than lower-extremity fractures, but that difference disappears when hand and finger injuries are excluded.
paper.methods: Retrospective comparative series using public NFL records and pro-football-reference statistics. Each injured player was matched to one control by position, age (±1 year), experience (±1 year) and preinjury performance, and a position-specific performance score was compared using paired t tests.
paper.findings: Of 37 players, 30 (81%) returned, with a mean time to return of 9.3 ± 8.2 months. Postinjury career length (4.3 vs 4.4 seasons), games per season (11.5 vs 11.3) and performance score (5.0 vs 4.7) did not differ from controls, and performance was similar to preinjury levels (5.0 vs 5.5). Upper-extremity fractures returned faster than lower-extremity fractures (4.0 ± 4.8 vs 14.6 ± 7.4 months, P = .00007) and scored higher postinjury (6.4 ± 4.3 vs 3.3 ± 2.1, P = .03), but these differences were not seen after hand and finger fractures were excluded.
paper.limitations: Data came from public online records, which carry selection, reporting and observer bias, and fracture details, classification and treatment were largely unavailable. The sample of 37 players is small, the authors note possible beta error, and offensive linemen performance scores, players still active and patient-reported outcomes were not assessed.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use the 81% return rate and the similar postinjury career length and performance scores to set realistic expectations for NFL players with open fractures. Four hand or finger fractures in this series were managed without surgery and those players returned, so nonoperative management may be considered case by case. The findings come from NFL players and may not transfer to other sports or levels.
paper.athleteDev: Performance scores in players who returned were close to their preinjury levels overall, which gives performance staff a reference for expected output after this injury at NFL level. The paper contains no training, load or monitoring data, and it does not score offensive linemen.
paper.rtp: The study can inform return-to-sport expectations: 30 of 37 NFL players (81%) played again, typically after about 9 months. It cannot set a return-to-play date for an individual athlete, because fracture grade, treatment and surgery timing are not available.

records.sourceFile: Performance and survivorship of NFL players with pectoralis major injuries.pdf

paper.citation: Bodendorfer BM, DeFroda SF, Shu HT, Knapik DM, Yang DS, Verma NN. Performance and Survivorship of National Football League Players with Pectoralis Major Injuries. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2021:e1-e8.
paper.abstract: This study used publicly available NFL data from the 1998 to 2020 seasons to examine return to play, performance and career length after pectoralis major injuries. It compared injury grades and operative with nonoperative management in 258 injuries. Most players returned to play, but return was lower and slower after surgical repair, and some defensive positions and wide receivers had lower performance scores after injury.
paper.tldr: NFL players with pectoralis major injuries returned to play less often and later after surgical repair, likely because repaired injuries were higher grade. Performance scores fell for some defensive positions and wide receivers after return, and career length did not differ by treatment.
paper.methods: Injuries were identified from weekly NFL injury reports and Pro-Football-Reference, verified with press releases, and graded from news reports or inferred from treatment and return. Player Efficiency Rating (PER) and Pro Football Focus (PFF) scores were compared for the season before injury and two seasons after, with Kaplan-Meier survival and log-rank tests for return to play and career length.
paper.findings: Of 258 injuries, 126 (48.8%) were repaired, 95.2% of them grade III, while none of the 116 nonoperatively treated injuries were grade III. Return to play was 85.3% overall, with 78.6% after repair vs 95.7% nonoperatively (P < .005), and mean return of 289.5 vs 47.4 days. PER was lower in the first postinjury season for overall defense (.32 to .28, P = .046) and defensive backs (.35 to .25, P = .049), and in the second season for defensive linemen (.38 to .27, P = .019) and wide receivers (6.68 to 3.58, P = .030); defensive linemen also had lower PFF grades in season 2 (P = .044), and career length did not differ by management (P = .980).
paper.limitations: Injuries came from public databases and some 'chest' or 'undisclosed' reports could not be confirmed, while grade was inferred from news reports and treatment. Operatively treated players had lower preinjury PER (P = .004), and the subgroup sizes are small. The abstract reports shorter career length for tears than strains (P < .001), but the results report no difference by degree of injury (P = .540), and the Discussion says only defensive linemen and wide receivers declined although Table 5 also shows first-season declines for overall defense and defensive backs; this summary follows the results and tables.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can expect a lower return-to-play rate and a longer time to return after surgical repair of pectoralis major injuries in NFL players, which in this sample mostly reflects higher-grade tears. Defensive players, especially defensive backs in the first season and defensive linemen in the second, and wide receivers in the second season showed lower PER or PFF scores, so their performance may be worth following after return. Career length did not differ by management in this sample.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use the position-specific PER and PFF declines (defensive backs and overall defense in season 1, defensive linemen and wide receivers in season 2) to plan follow-up after pectoralis major injury. PER is not defined for offensive linemen, and the paper reports no training, load or strength data.
paper.rtp: The study can inform return-to-sport expectations for NFL players: 85.3% returned overall, 78.6% after repair vs 95.7% nonoperatively, with mean return of 289.5 vs 47.4 days. It cannot set an individual return date or support a repair decision, because injury grade was inferred, the sample is NFL-only, and strength outcomes were not measured.
